{
  "hypothesis": "Predicted that limited time horizons at work would cause age-related differences in work motivation to be eliminated, specifically that younger workers' preferences would shift to resemble older workers' preferences for emotionally meaningful activities (helping colleagues) when time horizons are constrained.",
  "design": "mixed, with age as a continuous predictor and time horizon condition (unspecified, expanded, limited) as a between-subjects factor.",
  "manipulation_or_predictor": "Experimental manipulation of occupational time horizons via written prompts: 'unspecified' (imagining unscheduled time), 'expanded' (imagining staying with the company considerably longer), and 'limited' (imagining a contract expiring in a few months with a new job already offered).",
  "outcome_measure": "Forced-choice preference among three work-related activities: 'Help a colleague or a friend with a company project' (emotionally meaningful), 'Work on a project that may help you advance your career' (future-oriented), or 'Work on a project that may lead the company in a new direction' (future-oriented).",
  "population_and_setting": "Employed adults (full- or part-time) recruited via KnowledgePanel of GfK Research in the United States.",
  "sample_size_total": 555,
  "recruitment_and_incentive": "Recruited from a larger study about decisions and regret conducted by KnowledgePanel of GfK Research.",
  "analysis_plan": "Logistic regression to test the effect of age on the likelihood of choosing to help a colleague over future-oriented options, including Age x Condition interaction terms. Multinomial regression was used for post-hoc analysis of specific activity choices.",
  "preregistered_or_confirmatory": "not stated",
  "other_methods_notes": "The study used an adapted version of the Fredrickson and Carstensen (1990) social partner paradigm. Control variables included Future Time Perspective, education, and personality traits (Big-Five). An independent validation sample of 99 individuals was used to confirm that the experimental prompts and choice options were perceived as intended."
}
